And the alternative — not running the suites and merely asserting they were green — voids the project's own central premise and re-triggers ground rule 09.
fatal_flaws.can_it_be_fixed: Yes, and the fix is the same asset that fixes flaw #1: build the corpus from HIS OWN repositories. Acumen (2,621 tests, 28 adversarial reviews, pinned `==` deps, his personal project), Identity Reconciliation Engine, Smart Returns Resolver, Nistula Message Handler. He controls the licence, the environments are ones he can actually build on his own machine, the dependency pins already exist, AND he knows the ground truth of what each defect broke and why — which no public-repo miner has. Mix in 4-5 public cases and report catch rate split by source so cherry-picking is visible. Disclose the provenance loudly under ground rule 02 ('make it clear what existed before the competition'). One asset choice removes the schedule risk, the licensing objection, the ground-truth problem, and makes the 17 shippable.

fixable_weaknesses: THE BIGGEST SINGLE UPGRADE, and it is sitting unused in his dossier: replace 'every surviving finding must state a concrete failure scenario' (prose — unverifiable, LLM-graded, gameable) with his own defect-pin discipline: a finding is admitted ONLY if the agent produces an executable probe that FAILS on the buggy code and PASSES on the fix. This converts a soft prose requirement into a deterministic, judge-re-runnable, ungameable witness. It simultaneously (a) makes false positives structurally near-zero because unprovable findings are dropped by the system rather than counted, (b) gives him a mechanical match criterion so he never needs an LLM judge, (c) makes the whole result re-runnable from a clean environment, which is the #2 tie-break. It is his rarest technique and the proposal omits it entirely.

There are no clean, defect-free control cases in the corpus. Without them 'false-positive rate' has no denominator and cannot distinguish 'wrong' from 'found a second real bug'. Add 4 clean diffs to the 10+; report FP on those separately.

The FP guard has no pre-registered threshold and the PDF explicitly requires defining 'what a good final result looks like' BEFORE running. As written: catch 11/12 with 47 extra findings — is that a pass? Nothing answers that. Worse, the primary metric is effectively two metrics in tension, and the single-prompt baseline will naturally score BETTER on FP while worse on catch, so the results table shows a trade, not an improvement. Pre-register one combined metric ('verified defects caught, where unverified findings are not admitted') — the defect-pin gate makes that metric coherent.

'Anyone merging AI-written code' is the vaguest user in his entire portfolio, and it will be scored against a 15-point row that asks 'Who experiences the bottleneck?'. All three PDF appendix examples name a situated person with a decision and a cost of being wrong. He has that person and it is himself in May-August 2026: the solo engineer owning a production AI layer with real money moving through Razorpay and real promises made to guests, with no second engineer to review the merge. Name him. Price the miss.

The hot take as stated — 'a green test suite is not evidence of correctness' — is a 47-year-old truism (Dijkstra, 1969) and will score near zero on a row that asks for 'an observed failure mode turned into a practical lesson'. His actual measured finding is far sharper and genuinely non-obvious: roughly 30% of the blockers his gate caught were REGRESSIONS INTRODUCED BY THE PREVIOUS ROUND'S OWN FIX — the repair loop is itself a defect source. That is a real lesson about building reliable agents. He is shipping the dull half of his own insight.

Cost per task is a mandated row and a 4-6 agent architecture will lose it badly against a one-prompt baseline. With a flat-rate Claude Code subscription he has no bill, so he must impute cost from token counts at published API rates and disclose the imputation. Then own the loss explicitly in his 'states costs, not just benefits' voice: 'N times the tokens; break-even is one caught money-defect per M reviews.' Unaddressed, this row reads as a regression.

No removed experiment is planned. The PDF mandates one ('Include experiments you later removed and explain what they taught you'). The natural honest one is available for free: the skeptic pass will kill true findings as well as false ones — measure and report the recall it costs.
Human time per task must be instrumented from run 1, not retrofitted at hour 70.

Domain expertise — NSE F&O, hospitality PMS/booking, bilingual e-commerce triage, drilling NPT — is used at zero. The stated hard case ('reads as correct in isolation, only breaks across files') is literally the problem his Acumen parity harness was built to solve. A money-lens defect in P&L accounting across 188,345 trades is a hard case he can author with genuine authority and nobody can copy.
what_is_genuinely_strong: The problem is real and he has personally lived it, which is rare among 5,100 entrants who will mostly pick problems they have read about. The premise is not speculative for him — it is the documented history of his last two projects.

The shape fits the rubric well. Verification and orchestration are two of the six named capabilities, used for a stated reason rather than stacked for count, which satisfies the explicit anti-kitchen-sink warning. A defect-catch metric is objective, has a natural >=10-case corpus, and admits a hard case — the single hardest requirement in the brief is naturally satisfied.

Evaluation-first working is a genuine habit for him (78-dimension rubric, GroupKFold by wellbore, deliberately-reported weak baselines, independent recomputation in a separate session). The requirement that sinks most hackathon entries is his default mode.

His writing voice is a real, scarce asset against the 20-point anti-slop clause, and it transfers to any proposal — this is not a reason to prefer THIS proposal, but it is a reason his execution ceiling is higher than most entrants'.

The false-positive guard, though underspecified, shows the right instinct: he anticipated the obvious gaming of his own metric before anyone asked. That instinct is worth more than the current specification of it.
critiques.single_biggest_risk: He is entering the single most crowded lane in the field with a generic instantiation of it. 'AI code-review agent' is what a developer picks when told to solve a problem they understand, every entrant is a developer, and the PDF's own Appendix Example 1 is a code-analysis problem — meaning the archetype most likely to be copied is the one the judges pre-seeded. 'Multi-lens plus a skeptic critic' is the default multi-agent tutorial shape and will appear in dozens of submissions. The tie-break goes first to Agent Solution & Engineering, so being the 30th competent multi-lens reviewer is a mid-pack finish. Nothing in the proposal as written is hard for another entrant to produce by Sunday — while the two things that ARE hard to produce (a real longitudinal defect record from a shipped agentic system, and the defect-pin discipline that turns findings into executable witnesses) are both explicitly excluded from the build.
critiques.recommendation: Keep the problem. Re-ground the evidence base — this is 'keep with named changes', but the changes are load-bearing, not polish. Five changes, in priority order, all of which cost less time than the current plan: (1) Make the defect-pin the core mechanism, not the prose failure scenario: a finding is admitted only if the agent writes a probe that fails on the buggy code and passes on the fix. This is his rarest technique, it makes the metric deterministic and judge-re-runnable, and it is the one design decision in this project that another entrant will not think of. (2) Build the corpus primarily from his OWN repositories (Acumen, Identity Reconciliation, Smart Returns, Nistula Message Handler), disclosed openly under ground rule 02, with 4-5 public cases mixed in and results reported split by source. This kills the schedule risk, the licensing objection and the ground-truth problem in one move. (3) Ship the 17 defects as minimal synthetic repros with green suites around them — turning his anecdote into data — or at minimum derive the review lenses from that taxonomy and say so, so the 30-point row sees an evidence-grounded design choice instead of a guess. (4) Replace 'anyone merging AI-written code' with the solo engineer shipping agent-written code into production with money moving through it and no second reviewer — a person he can name, whose cost of a miss he can price. (5) Replace the truism hot take with his actual finding: agent-authored fixes are themselves a leading source of new blockers, roughly one in three in his record — the repair loop needs its own gate. Add 4 clean control cases, pre-register the pass bar, plan the skeptic's recall cost as the mandatory removed experiment. Executed as specified today: ~68, respectable, mid-pack. Executed with these five changes: low-to-mid 80s and genuinely in contention, because every one of them is something the other 5,099 entrants structurally cannot copy.

alternatives.angle: micro1-fit. The three PDF appendix examples are not three domains, they are one archetype wearing three coats: a judgement that a paid human expert currently makes, that experts make inconsistently, scored by agreement with a human panel (Ex.1 rank correlation) or by self-consistency across items (Ex.3 memory trap), with uncertainty surfaced and the human left as decider (Ex.2). That archetype is not a coincidence — it is micro1's P&L. They sell expert judgement converted into training data, evals and feedback loops; they buy agent traces at $2-15 each; their validation screen this week is literally trace integrity and reproducibility checks. So the highest-resonance move is to take a step of micro1's own production pipeline — authoring eval items, grading at scale, verifying agent output — and prove an agent does it closer to a human panel than a naive prompt. The de-pandering rule I applied: never name micro1, never touch the AI-recruiter domain the PDF warns about, and always anchor the metric to a human panel someone ELSE paid for and published, so the ground truth is not the contestant's own invention. That last point is where Review Gate is weakest: its corpus of seeded bugs is a ruler the contestant made himself. All three candidates below replace self-made ground truth with an external, already-purchased human panel or a mechanical oracle. Candidate 1 is Ex.1's archetype (rank correlation vs 93 paid developers), Candidate 2 is Ex.3's (a metric one prompt structurally cannot win), Candidate 3 is Ex.2's (visible uncertainty, abstention, human decides) — deliberately one per example, so whichever he picks, a judge reading the appendix recognises the shape.

candidates.name: Intake — screening eval tasks before they cost expert time
candidates.one_line: Screens candidate agent-eval tasks (a GitHub issue, its repo, its tests) for the flaws that make a benchmark item unusable, and ranks them the way a panel of 93 paid professional developers ranked the same tasks.
candidates.intended_user: The person who builds evaluation sets for a frontier lab, and the benchmark author. Concretely: someone holding 400 candidate GitHub issues with budget to have domain experts hand-verify 50 of them, who must choose which 50. Secondary user: any team that reports a benchmark number and would like to know whether the ruler is straight.
candidates.bottleneck: Screening candidate eval items is the expensive human step and it does not scale. OpenAI paid 93 Python developers to screen 1,699 SWE-bench samples; the result was that 38.3% had underspecified problem statements and 61.1% had tests that could unfairly fail a valid solution. Two reviewers reading the same issue disagree about whether it is specified enough to test on, because the judgement is 'could a competent engineer have known to write this exact behaviour from this text alone', which is genuinely contested. Ship a bad item and every model's measured score moves in a direction nobody can see, and the error is invisible forever because the benchmark becomes the definition of correct.
candidates.baseline: Type 2 — one general purpose agent with basic tools. It receives the issue text, the gold patch and the FAIL_TO_PASS test bodies pasted in, and returns two severity scores 0-3 (issue underspecified, tests unfair) with a sentence of reasoning. Same cases, same output schema, same scoring script as the final solution. Resource difference to disclose: the advanced solution may clone the repository; the baseline sees only pasted text.
candidates.advanced_solution: Four purposeful additions, each earning a changelog row. (1) Context: clone the repo at the base commit, read the actual implementation the tests exercise and the tests that already existed, so 'unfair' is judged against the project's own conventions rather than in the abstract. (2) Skill, a specification lens: the agent attempts to write the patch from the issue text ALONE and logs every decision the issue failed to determine — exact function name, error string, boundary behaviour. Underspecification becomes a count of forced free choices, not a vibe. (3) Skill, a test-fairness lens: diff what the FAIL_TO_PASS tests assert against what the issue actually requests, flagging every assertion on a detail the issue never mentions. (4) Verification, in deterministic code: a flag survives only if it quotes one line from the issue and one line from the test or repo; unquoted flags are dropped before the human ever sees them. Output is a review queue sorted by expected review value, each row carrying a severity, its two quoted anchors, and a 'reviewers will likely split here' marker. The human accepts or discards; the tool never rejects an item itself.
candidates.primary_metric: Spearman rank correlation with the 3-annotator ensembled human severity, computed separately for the two criteria, on the same held-out instances for baseline and solution. Reported alongside the decision metric the user actually buys on: precision@40, the fraction of the top 40 queued items that carry a severe human label (>=2). Hard to game because the two pull opposite ways — flagging everything destroys the ranking, flagging nothing destroys recall, and the ordering is what the metric reads. Also reported: human minutes per item, timed against his own hand-screening of 10 items done first with a stopwatch, and cost per item.
candidates.eval_corpus: OpenAI's public release of human annotations over SWE-bench test samples: 1,699 samples, each labelled independently by 3 of 93 professional Python developers, with per-criterion severity 0-3 and a published conservative ensembling rule (max severity across the 3). Fully public, produced and paid for by someone else. Split: 40 instances as a development set for prompt work, then 12 held-out cases of 10 instances each, stratified by source repository so no single project drives the result. Repos are cloned from public GitHub at pinned base commits — no Docker, no install. A 13th case of 20 freshly-scraped open issues from live public repos is run to show the screener is not SWE-bench-shaped, though it has no human labels and is reported as qualitative only.
candidates.hard_case: The batch of instances where the three human annotators disagreed by two or more severity points on the same criterion. The correct behaviour is not to guess the ensemble but to raise the disagreement marker. What it should reveal, and what makes it worth writing up: the agent's confident calls are accurate and its errors concentrate precisely where the humans also split, which is simultaneously the honest limitation and the argument for keeping a qualified reviewer in the loop rather than automating the accept.
candidates.hot_take: Before you measure the agent, measure the ruler. In the most-cited coding benchmark in the field, the people paid to check it flagged 38% of problem statements as underspecified and 61% of test suites as capable of failing a correct fix — and we kept quoting the scores anyway. A large share of what we call model error is task error we agreed not to look at.
candidates.why_this_beats_review_gate: Review Gate's ground truth is a corpus the contestant seeded himself, which is the one thing a sharp judge will push on: seeded bugs are easier and more uniform than real ones, and the catch rate is a self-graded exam. Intake's ground truth is 93 paid professional developers, three per sample, released by a third party, with the inter-annotator disagreement published — so the metric is rank agreement with a human panel, which is verbatim the technique the PDF's own first example prescribes ('have qualified reviewers rank ten approved codebases... does the agent come closer to the reviewers' order'). Crowding is far lower: in a field of engineers, 'multi-agent code review' is the single most predictable submission; a tool that audits benchmarks is not. And the domain is quality control on evaluation data, which is micro1's product rather than an adjacent engineering nicety. Chinmoy also keeps his real advantage — his review-gate war story becomes the README's origin paragraph rather than uncitable evidence.

candidates.name: Precedent — the grader that does not drift
candidates.one_line: A rubric-grading agent that cites its own prior rulings, so item 200 in a queue is scored by the same standard as item 3, shipped with a consistency audit that shows the reader their current judge is not.
candidates.intended_user: Anyone who runs a grading queue at scale: a data lab scoring expert submissions before delivery, a team running LLM-as-judge over thousands of model outputs, an operations lead who has to defend a score to the person who received it. The sharpest version of this user is the one whose grade decides a payment or a rejection.
candidates.bottleneck: Grading standards drift, and no accuracy metric can see it. The same answer scores differently depending on what was graded immediately before it, which side of a pair it appeared on, and how deep into the batch it sits. A judge can agree with humans 80% of the time and still contradict itself on a third of the items it sees twice, because those are different measurements. Averaged over a batch the drift cancels and looks like noise; to the individual whose submission was rejected it is the whole story. When a client asks 'why did this one score 3 and that one score 5', 'I cannot reproduce my own grade' is the answer that loses the contract.
candidates.baseline: Type 1 — one direct prompt with basic instructions. The standard single-call judge: rubric, the two responses, 'which is better and why'. Identical model, identical rubric text, identical cases as the final solution. The only disclosed resource difference is that the advanced solution makes a second swapped-order call and retrieves prior gradings, so its token cost per item is roughly 3x — reported in the cost-per-task row rather than hidden.
candidates.advanced_solution: Three purposeful capabilities, chosen because each fixes an observed failure. (1) Memory, as case law rather than cache: a precedent store holds every prior ruling with its score and its stated reason; before grading, the k nearest prior cases are retrieved and the grader must either follow them or state in one sentence why this case is distinguishable. (2) Verification: every judgement is re-run with the two responses swapped, and disagreement between the two orders is a hard failure that forces an explicit tie or escalates to an adjudication pass — position bias becomes a caught error instead of a silent one. (3) A deterministic consistency checker in ordinary code, not a prompt: it builds the comparison graph, finds cycles (A>B, B>C, C>A) and precedent contradictions, and only the contradictions pay for a second expensive pass. The shipped artifact is the graded queue plus a consistency report an ops lead can hand to a client, every score linked to the precedents it followed and the ones it declined.
candidates.primary_metric: Agreement with the expert human votes, gated at zero self-contradiction. Formally: human-agreement rate on the pairs, with any run whose self-contradiction rate (order-flip disagreements + graph cycles + repeat-item disagreements) exceeds a threshold fixed before the run declared failing regardless of its agreement number. Two numbers, one gate. You cannot buy agreement by being erratic, and you cannot buy consistency by answering 'tie' every time, because ties cost agreement. Published human-human agreement on this corpus is ~81%, so the ceiling is known and the result is interpretable rather than self-referential.
candidates.eval_corpus: lmsys/mt_bench_human_judgments: 3.3K expert-level pairwise human preferences over 6 models on 80 MT-Bench questions, annotated mostly by graduate students in the topic area of each question, with human-human agreement published at ~81%. Licence is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — must be declared in the README and flagged against the hackathon's IP clause; the MIT-licensed Anthropic/hh-rlhf preference set is the drop-in fallback if the NC term is a problem, and both are cheap to wire to the same harness. Cases: 12 queue batches of ~60 pairs, grouped by MT-Bench category (writing, roleplay, reasoning, math, coding, extraction, STEM, humanities), with two kinds of probe planted inside each batch — the same pair re-inserted 40 positions later, and every pair's mirror image.
candidates.hard_case: A planted near-duplicate: an item textually almost identical to one graded 40 positions earlier, differing in exactly one substantive way (the preferred response's code now carries an off-by-one). A naive precedent store follows precedent and gets it confidently wrong — which is the entire reason the 'is this distinguishable, and why' step exists. What it reveals is the honest cost of the headline feature: memory buys consistency, and consistency without an argued distinction is just being reliably wrong. That single case justifies the design and indicts the naive version of it in the same breath.
candidates.hot_take: Your LLM judge is not biased, it is unreliable, and every accuracy number you own is hiding it. Measure a judge against itself before you measure it against humans — the drift is invisible in the mean and it is the only part the person being graded can feel.
candidates.why_this_beats_review_gate: Review Gate's improvement lives on an axis a well-written single prompt can plausibly contest, so its baseline looks like a straw man the moment a judge asks 'what if the one prompt were good'. Precedent's improvement is on an axis a single prompt structurally cannot win: one stateless call has no way to know what it decided 40 items ago, so cross-item consistency is not a harder version of the baseline task, it is a task the baseline cannot attempt. That is exactly the shape the PDF's third example endorses ('each sentence can be correct while the series as a whole no longer feels coherent'), which means a judge reading the appendix recognises the move. It also puts micro1's core mechanism — human preference judgement at scale — under the microscope without touching the recruiting product the brief warns against, and the human ceiling is published so the number means something.

candidates.name: Verdict — merging agent code when there is no oracle
candidates.one_line: Given an issue and an agent-written patch and no hidden tests, decide merge, hold or reject — by writing down what the fix must do before looking at what was written, then scoring the patch against that.
candidates.intended_user: Anyone merging agent output at volume where an acceptance test does not exist, which is nearly all real work: the FAIL_TO_PASS test only exists inside benchmarks. Directly: a lab or data vendor grading agent runs where re-running the full harness is impossible, too slow or too expensive, and an engineer must sign off on the patch itself.
candidates.bottleneck: A patch that reads plausibly and a patch that fixes the bug are indistinguishable at a glance, and the reviewer has no oracle to appeal to. So the reviewer either merges on vibes or spends twenty minutes reconstructing the failure by hand to build a private oracle, then throws it away. Both scale badly. Worse, reading the diff first is an act of persuasion: once you have seen a confident fix you are evaluating whether you can find fault with it, not whether it does the job. Reviewer verdicts on the same patch disagree for exactly that reason.
candidates.baseline: Type 2 — one general purpose agent with basic tools. It receives the issue text and the patch and returns merge / reject plus a confidence. Same 120 triples, same output schema, same scorer. Disclosed resource difference: the advanced solution may clone and read the repository at the base commit; the baseline sees only the two pasted texts. Both are denied the hidden tests, because the hidden tests are the answer key.
candidates.advanced_solution: Ordering is the whole idea, and each step maps to one named capability. (1) Context and tools: shallow-clone the repo at the base commit, locate the symbol the issue names, read the surrounding implementation and the tests that already cover it — read-only, no install, no Docker. (2) Skill: derive a reproduction spec from the issue ALONE, inputs to expected output, before the patch is ever loaded, so the standard is fixed independently of the thing being judged. (3) Verification: check the patch against the spec clause by clause, and separately run two deterministic cheat probes in code — does the patch touch test files, and does it special-case the exact literals quoted in the issue. (4) Abstention: the answer space is merge / hold / reject-with-reason, hold is a first-class outcome that routes to a human, and no consequential action is taken by the tool. Ground rules 04 and 05 are satisfied by the design rather than by a disclaimer.
candidates.primary_metric: Precision on the merge verdict at a coverage floor fixed before the run: of the triples the system agrees to decide (target coverage >=60%), what fraction of its merges actually resolved the issue, scored against SWE-bench's hidden-test labels. Gaming is closed from both sides — abstaining broadly collapses coverage below the floor and the run does not count; merging everything collapses precision. Reported alongside: reviewer minutes per patch (timed on 10 patches he reviews by hand first), cost per patch, and the coverage-precision curve rather than a single point, so the reader can pick their own operating point.
candidates.eval_corpus: The public SWE-bench/experiments repository, which hosts open-sourced predictions, execution logs and trajectories for leaderboard submissions: every submission ships logs/<instance>/patch.diff plus report.json carrying the resolved verdict produced by actually running the hidden tests. Draw 120 (issue, patch, label) triples balanced roughly 50/50 resolved/unresolved, spread across at least four distinct agent submissions so the result is not a study of one agent's style, and restricted to pure-Python repos that clone in seconds. Cases: 12 batches of 10, one per repo-by-agent stratum. Every label is external, mechanical, and was produced by someone else's test harness on someone else's patch — no bug in this corpus was planted by the contestant.
candidates.hard_case: A matched pair of documented pathologies: an unresolved patch that is semantically reasonable and fails only an over-specific assertion, and a resolved patch that passes for the wrong reason. Both phenomena are documented in the SWE-bench literature. What it reveals is uncomfortable and worth leading with: the label is not truth, it is what the hidden tests said, and an honest system has to be able to output 'this fix is correct and the benchmark will mark it wrong'. That case is where the primary metric and the right answer come apart, and saying so out loud is worth more than the point it costs.
candidates.hot_take: Reviewing a diff is the wrong job. Write down what the fix must do before you look at what was written, or you are not reviewing, you are being persuaded — and an agent that has already produced a confident patch is very good at persuading.
candidates.why_this_beats_review_gate: It keeps Review Gate's real instinct — a green signal is not proof — and removes its single most attackable part. Nothing is seeded: the bugs are real, the patches were written by other people's agents, and the verdicts come from a test harness the contestant never touched, so the catch-rate number stops being a self-graded exam. The output is also an operations decision under an abstention budget rather than a list of findings, which makes the metric one an engineering manager would actually buy on and makes 'flag everything' structurally unprofitable instead of merely discouraged. It sits nearer the crowded lane than the other two candidates, and that is the honest cost of it: 'agent reviews code' will be a common submission, and this must win on the corpus and the abstention framing rather than on novelty. Its planned removed experiment is unusually good — bolt on real execution inside prebuilt Docker images for a 12-instance subset, predict several hours of environment work for a metric move too small to be significant on a subset that size, then report the hours and cut it. If it does pay off it becomes the headline; either way the changelog gets an honest negative row that cost real time.

alternatives.angle: Measurability. I judged every idea by one test: can a judge who does not trust me re-derive the headline number by running a program, and can I state — before any run — the structural reason the sanctioned baseline cannot reach it? Review Gate fails both. Its catch rate is scored by matching free-text findings against known defects, which needs an LLM judge or my own hand, so the number is a judgement call I made about my own system. Its corpus needs historical OSS test suites to actually build and run inside 28 hours, which is a dependency swamp. Its second guard metric (false-positive rate) turns the result into a two-number tradeoff a skeptical judge can argue with rather than a single number they can check. And "agentic code review" is the single most predictable response to this brief — with 5,100 entrants, the judges will read it dozens of times before lunch. All three alternatives below replace the LLM judge with a program (a mutation runner, a stopwatch plus a correctness gate, a third party's own filed numbers), and in each case the baseline's failure has a one-sentence cause I can state in advance. Ranked for the actual tie-break order: Stopwatch and Sharpen carry the strongest Agent Engineering story because the agent's loop is closed by an executable oracle rather than by its own opinion; Tie-Out carries the strongest Reproducibility story because the answer key was authored by somebody else and is downloadable in thirty seconds.

candidates.name: Stopwatch
candidates.one_line: An optimization agent that is only allowed to keep changes it measured — every candidate edit is benchmarked and reverted unless the win survives a pre-registered threshold and the correctness gate.
candidates.intended_user: The engineer who owns a batch job, CI stage, or data pipeline whose runtime has crept from 8 minutes to 40, and who now gets AI-suggested optimizations they cannot safely merge. They need speedups they can trust not to have quietly changed behavior — and they need to know which suggestions to throw away.
candidates.bottleneck: Optimizing code is a measurement problem that both humans and LLMs solve by pattern-matching instead. The model recognizes a shape it has seen (loop to vectorized, add a cache, swap a data structure), applies it, and writes a confident paragraph explaining the speedup. Nobody times it. At the actual input sizes the pipeline runs, a meaningful share of those edits are neutral or slower, and some pass the unit tests while breaking a contract the tests never pinned (sort stability, iteration order, float accumulation order). The engineer's real cost is not the slow code; it is reviewing a pile of plausible diffs with no evidence attached to any of them.
candidates.baseline: Type 2 — one general-purpose agent with basic tools: file read/edit plus a test runner, so it can verify correctness but has no benchmark harness and no way to measure the effect of its own edit. Same model, same task, same cases; the only withheld resource is measurement, which makes the attribution of the improvement unambiguous.
candidates.advanced_solution: A closed measurement loop: profile the target under the case's real workload, form one hypothesis, apply it in an isolated worktree, run the correctness gate (unit tests plus a per-case property/invariant test), then benchmark against the pinned baseline with repeated interleaved trials. Keep the edit only if the median speedup clears the pre-registered threshold and the trial distributions do not overlap; otherwise revert and record the rejected hypothesis in a per-case memory file so the next round does not re-try it. Capabilities used and defended: tools (profiler, benchmark runner, test runner), verification (correctness gate plus measured-win gate before any edit is retained), memory (the rejected-hypothesis ledger). No orchestration, and the README says why it was not needed.
candidates.primary_metric: Trusted speedup: geometric mean of per-case speedup across all cases, where any case that fails the correctness gate is scored 1.00x (no credit for a fast wrong answer) and any case made slower keeps its true sub-1.0 factor. One number, produced by a stopwatch, that punishes ambition without evidence. Reported alongside it as guards: regressions shipped (count of cases left slower than they started) and correctness failures. Pre-registered 'good' before any run: >=1.5x trusted speedup, 0 regressions, 0 correctness failures. Gaming is structurally blocked — you cannot win by hedging (no edit means 1.00x) and you cannot win by cheating (the gate zeroes it).
candidates.eval_corpus: 12 self-contained Python tasks, each = target module + workload generator + unit tests + one invariant/property test. Six lifted from permissively licensed public repos (pure-Python reference implementations and known-slow paths; fetched by pinned version at setup rather than vendored, with licenses recorded). Six authored synthetic tasks, each documenting the real-world archetype it models (N+1 lookup in a loop, repeated recompilation inside a hot path, quadratic string building, dict rebuilt per iteration, JSON re-parsed per record, sort called inside a scan). Ground rule 07 explicitly permits synthetic; the split is disclosed per case in the results table. Assembly: roughly 4-5 hours, zero external services, no network at eval time — which also makes the judge's re-run deterministic.
candidates.hard_case: A case where the textbook optimization is a regression. A per-row transform over batches of ~40 elements: converting the Python loop to a vectorized NumPy call is the move every model reaches for, and at that array size the per-call overhead makes it ~1.6x slower. The second-obvious move — memoizing on an unhashable-ish composite key — is faster but changes tie-breaking order in a way the unit tests do not catch and only the invariant test does. It is the one case that separates a system that reasons about performance from one that measures it, and I expect the baseline to ship both mistakes with a confident rationale for each.
candidates.hot_take: An agent without a stopwatch is a reliable source of confident regressions. In the baseline run, every slower-than-before edit arrived with a paragraph explaining why it was faster — the prose quality was uncorrelated with the direction of the change. The lesson generalizes past performance work: whenever an agent's claim is cheap to verify with a tool and expensive to verify by reading, the tool must be inside the loop, not in the review afterwards, because the explanation will be equally fluent either way.
candidates.why_this_beats_review_gate: The headline number is a physical measurement plus a binary gate, not an LLM's opinion about whether a finding matches a defect — a judge re-runs one command and watches the same number appear. The baseline's failure has a stated structural cause (it cannot observe the effect of its own edit) rather than an empirical hope that the model is bad at reviewing diffs; with n=10 seeded defects, Review Gate's delta could easily land inside the noise. The corpus needs no historical OSS test suites to resurrect, no fix-commit mining, and no 'was the suite really green' precondition to verify — the largest schedule risk in Review Gate is deleted outright. It is also visible in seconds: two bars and a regressions-shipped counter, with the baseline's own confident rationale for its slowest edit quoted underneath. And it is nowhere near the crowded lane; a code-review agent is what most of 5,100 entrants will hand in.

candidates.name: Sharpen
candidates.one_line: A test-hardening agent that strengthens a weak suite against mutation, and is scored only on mutants it was never allowed to see.
candidates.intended_user: The tech lead whose team now merges AI-written tests. The PR shows 94% line coverage and a green run, and they have no way to answer the only question that matters: if someone broke this code tomorrow, would any of these tests notice?
candidates.bottleneck: Coverage measures which lines were visited, not which defects would be caught, and AI-generated tests are systematically assertion-poor — they execute a lot and assert little, which is precisely the pattern coverage rewards. Reviewing a 400-line generated test file by hand to find the assertions that pin nothing takes longer than writing the tests, so nobody does it, and the suite becomes a badge instead of a safety net. The team keeps shipping regressions through a green pipeline and blames the code.
candidates.baseline: Type 1 — one direct prompt with basic instructions: the module, its existing tests, and 'add tests to strengthen this suite.' No tools, no execution, no mutation feedback. A second reference point is also reported (not the sanctioned baseline, just an exhibit): a coverage-driven pass instructed to reach 100% line coverage, which is what the intended user's current tooling actually rewards.
candidates.advanced_solution: A closed loop against an executable oracle. A deterministic AST mutation engine generates the mutant catalog per module with a seeded, committed split: ~70% visible, ~30% held out and never exposed. The agent gets a tool that runs the visible surviving mutants and returns which ones its new tests killed, plus a hard verification gate — every submitted test must pass against pristine, unmutated source (a suite that breaks the module scores the case zero) and each mutant runs in a subprocess under a timeout so a mutation-induced infinite loop cannot be scored as a kill. The agent iterates: run, read survivors, write targeted tests, re-run, and for anything it cannot kill it must file an equivalent-mutant claim with a written argument. Capabilities: tools (mutation runner, test runner), verification (pristine-source gate plus the held-out split), skills (a mutation-operator-to-assertion playbook added at iteration 2). Cross-checked against a pinned third-party mutation tool on two modules so the scorer is not only mine.
candidates.primary_metric: Held-out mutation kill rate — the percentage of mutants killed on the ~30% of the catalog the agent never saw and never ran against, averaged across cases, with any case whose tests fail on pristine source scored 0%. Pre-registered 'good': >=70% held-out kill rate with zero broken suites. The held-out split is the anti-gaming device: iterating against the score is impossible because the score lives on mutants outside the feedback loop, so the only way to raise it is to write tests that genuinely pin behavior. Also reported: visible-vs-held-out gap (the overfitting measurement itself), tests added, suite runtime added, human minutes per module, cost per module.
candidates.eval_corpus: 10-12 pure-Python modules with real, human-written partial test suites, fetched by pinned version from PyPI sdists at setup (semver comparison, duration parsing, interval merging, retry/backoff policy, human-readable formatting, CSV dialect handling, and similar single-purpose permissive libraries) — no vendoring, licenses recorded, no heavy dependencies so a judge's clean environment installs in a minute. Where a chosen module ships no tests, a deliberately thin starter suite is authored to mirror a real under-tested repo, and every such case is labeled as authored in the results table. Assembly: ~3 hours, mostly picking modules whose test suites actually run offline.
candidates.hard_case: A module whose surviving mutants include genuine equivalent mutants — semantically identical to the original, unkillable by any test. The right answer is to stop and say so with an argument. It is the case that punishes flailing, and it is where I expect the ugliest failure mode: an agent that cannot kill a mutant starts weakening its own assertions or asserting on implementation details to make the number move. Whatever it does there goes in the report verbatim.
candidates.hot_take: A test suite is not an asset until something has tried to break it, and an agent scored on mutants it was allowed to see will overfit to them exactly as a student overfits to the practice exam. The generalizable rule: when you give an agent a feedback tool, hold back a slice of the signal and score on that instead — the gap between the visible score and the held-out score is a direct, cheap measurement of how much of your agent's performance is real.
candidates.why_this_beats_review_gate: It attacks the same conviction Review Gate is built on — a green suite is not evidence — but replaces the soft instrument with a hard one. Instead of an LLM adjudicating whether a free-text finding corresponds to a known defect, a mutation runner returns a boolean per mutant, and the primary number is computed on mutants withheld from the agent, which is a stronger anti-gaming guarantee than any false-positive guard rail. The corpus needs no fix-commit archaeology and no 'the suite must still pass after injection' precondition; the mutation engine produces its cases deterministically and commits them. It also produces a single devastating exhibit for the video — 100% line coverage next to a sub-50% kill rate on the same file — which lands in about two seconds. Crowding-wise, test generation is a common lane but mutation-scored, held-out-split test generation is not, and the honest risk is that a judge skimming the title files it next to twenty 'AI writes tests' entries before reading the split.

candidates.name: Tie-Out
candidates.one_line: A filing-extraction agent whose every number is checked against arithmetic that must tie, and graded against the filer's own XBRL tags — an answer key I did not author.
candidates.intended_user: The analyst or data engineer who has to turn a quarter's worth of 10-Qs into a spreadsheet by Monday. They are not confused by the finance; they are being destroyed by scale, sign and period conventions across ten documents from ten issuers who each format differently.
candidates.bottleneck: The errors in long-document financial extraction are not random and do not shrink with a bigger context window, because they are not attention failures — they are convention failures. 'In thousands, except per share data' sits in a header forty pages from the table. Parentheses mean negative. A single 10-Q carries three-month and nine-month columns for the same line item, plus prior-year comparatives, and picking the wrong column is a wrong number that reads perfectly. I confirmed this in the source data before proposing it: Apple's latest 10-Q tags diluted EPS as both 6.88 and 2.02 under the same accession number, and only the period bounds distinguish them. A single wrong scale factor propagates through every downstream model, and the analyst catches it — if they catch it — by noticing the totals do not add up.
candidates.baseline: Type 1 — one direct prompt with basic instructions: the full filing text in a single large context window, plus the schema of facts to extract, no tools. Deliberately generous — the whole document fits, so no truncation objection is available — which makes the resulting failure a statement about convention handling rather than about context length.
candidates.advanced_solution: Retrieval to the specific statement table rather than the whole filing; a normalization skill that resolves scale, sign convention and period bounds as explicit fields before a value is accepted; and a deterministic tie-out verifier that runs the arithmetic a human analyst runs — gross profit equals revenue minus cost of sales, segment revenues sum to consolidated, assets equal liabilities plus equity, the three-month figures across quarters sum to the year-to-date figure. A failed tie-out is not a warning; it forces targeted re-extraction of only the offending facts. Cross-filing memory carries each issuer's resolved conventions and prior-period figures forward, so the current filing's comparative column is checked against what the issuer actually reported at the time, and a genuine mismatch is surfaced as a suspected restatement rather than silently overwritten. Capabilities: context (targeted retrieval), skills (the normalizer), verification (the tie-out loop), memory (cross-filing conventions and prior figures).
candidates.primary_metric: Exact-fact accuracy against the filer's own XBRL: percentage of the fact set matched exactly on normalized value, sign and period bounds, graded automatically against data.sec.gov companyfacts filtered by accession number. No partial credit, no rubric, no judge. Abstention is closed off — a fact marked 'not disclosed' that the filer did in fact tag counts as wrong — so hedging cannot buy safety. Pre-registered 'good': >=90% exact-fact accuracy with zero unflagged tie-out violations. Secondary: tie-out violations remaining in the delivered output, and cross-filing coherence violations.
candidates.eval_corpus: 10-12 filings across 10 issuers and 3 sectors, drawn from EDGAR: the filing HTML from the public archives, the answer key from the free companyfacts JSON API keyed by accession number (verified live during this analysis — HTTP 200, 503 us-gaap concepts for a single issuer, every fact carrying start/end/accn/form). Roughly 20 facts per filing gives 200+ independently gradable data points, comfortably past the 10-case floor at the filing level and far past it at the fact level. Setup requires only a declared User-Agent header, no key, no account, no cost. Corpus build: 3-4 hours, and the fetch script is itself a deliverable so the judge rebuilds the corpus from scratch rather than trusting my copy.
candidates.hard_case: An issuer that changed its segment reporting between the prior-year comparative and the current period, so the prior figures in this filing legitimately differ from the numbers the same issuer filed a year ago. The naive cross-filing check calls it an error; the correct behavior is to flag it as a reporting change with both sources cited and defer to the human. It is the case that tests whether the memory capability produces judgement or just a mismatch counter, and the one place in the project where the honest output is 'a person needs to look at this.'
candidates.hot_take: Long-document extraction errors are not attention failures, so throwing context at them does not help — they are convention failures in scale, sign and period, they are systematically wrong in the same direction, and three lines of arithmetic that must tie catches more of them than any amount of additional context. I intend to prove that as a removed experiment rather than assert it: the whole-filing-in-one-window variant is already scheduled to be built, measured and cut.
candidates.why_this_beats_review_gate: The grading key was written by the filer and published by the SEC — I could not tilt it if I wanted to, and a judge can pull the same JSON in one curl and re-grade my output independently. That is the strongest Reproducibility artifact available in this competition, and Reproducibility is the second tie-break. Review Gate's key, by contrast, is defects I mined or seeded myself, matched to findings by a judge I also configured. Exact-fact accuracy is also a single unambiguous percentage where catch-rate-guarded-by-false-positive-rate is two numbers in tension that a skeptical judge can argue about. The premise here needs no personal anecdote to support it — the period ambiguity is visible in the raw data in ten seconds. Being harsh about it: this idea's surface is the most crowded genre in the whole hackathon. Document extraction with retrieval is what a large fraction of 5,100 entrants will build, and my defense is entirely in the second paragraph a judge reads — the third-party answer key and the tie-out loop — not in the pitch. If a judge stops at the title, this loses to Stopwatch.

scores.candidate_name: Intake — screening eval tasks before they cost expert time
scores.strongest_argument_for:
The ground truth is the best available to any entrant in this event, and I verified it rather than trusting the pitch. OpenAI's zip (cdn.openai.com/introducing-swe-bench-verified/swe-bench-annotation-results.zip) ships BOTH ensembled_annotations_public.csv (1,699 rows) and samples_with_3_annotations_public.csv (5,097 rows = 1,699 x 3) with user_id, per-annotator 0-3 severities, per-annotator free-text notes, annotator_confidence, and claimed_at/submitted_at timestamps across 93 distinct annotators. Every factual claim in the pitch holds: ensemble == max-of-3 matches on 1,699/1,699 for both criteria; underspecified>=2 is 38.3%; false_negative>=2 is 61.2%.

That file lets him do something almost no other entry can: pin BOTH ends of the scale on the same axis as his agent. I computed the numbers in ~15 minutes. Leave-one-out single-human Spearman against max-of-the-other-two is 0.376 (underspecification) and 0.455 (test fairness). Random-order precision@40 on a 120-pool is 0.301 / 0.537; a single paid professional gets 0.474 / 0.804; oracle is 0.99 / 1.00. A results table reading "random floor / baseline / agent / paid professional / oracle" executes the PDF's own Example 1 technique ("have qualified reviewers rank ten approved codebases... does the agent come closer to the reviewers' order") more rigorously than the example itself, and it converts a small absolute Spearman into a legible claim: "reaches X% of the level a paid professional Python developer reaches against the same panel."

Second: judge alignment is the strongest of any plausible candidate. micro1 self-describes as "the leading AI data lab for training frontier models and evaluating AI agents." The user is literally the judge's own job function, and the bottleneck is quantified by a third party who paid for it (5,097 annotations, median 119 minutes claimed-to-submitted per annotation, n=3,636 from the timestamps). Third: ground rules 04 and 05 (sandboxed consequential actions, qualified human reviewer) are satisfied by construction — the tool ranks, the human accepts or discards, it never rejects an item — where most entrants will fumble this. Fourth: no Docker, no install, one public zip, text-in/JSON-out; that is a genuinely rare reproducibility position for anything SWE-bench-adjacent.
scores.strongest_argument_against:
The project whose entire thesis is "audit your ground truth" does not audit its own, and the specific hole is fatal under cross-examination.

All 500 SWE-bench Verified instances are a strict subset of the 539 filter_out==False instances (I checked: overlap 500/500). So the single most-mirrored eval artifact in the field — 321k downloads on one HuggingFace mirror, plus Kaggle, plus dozens of GitHub forks, public since August 2024 — is a near-perfect key to the label. A model that does nothing but recall Verified-500 membership and rank non-members first scores: 97.7% accuracy on filter_out, 90.6% on the false_negative>=2 binary, and precision 0.867 on false_negative against a 0.612 random floor. That 0.867 BEATS the 0.804 that a real leave-one-out human annotator achieves. Memorization outperforms a paid professional on his headline decision metric, with zero reasoning. The word "contamination" does not appear once in the proposal. A micro1 judge — an AI data lab that builds evals for a living — is the single audience most certain to ask this in the first two minutes, and "my agent ranks eval items well" collapses into "Claude remembers which ones OpenAI kept."

The metric also has no statistical power as specified. I bootstrapped it: at n=120 held-out the 95% CI width on Spearman is 0.33 (underspecification) and 0.31 (test fairness) — wider than the entire distance from zero to the human ceiling of 0.376/0.455. A baseline-to-solution delta of +0.06 is invisible. Per-case Spearman at n=10 has sd 0.29-0.32, so the "12 cases of 10" structure is a checkbox for the PDF's >=10-cases rule, not science. And the stratification is literally unbuildable as written: "12 held-out cases of 10 instances each, stratified by source repository" — there are 12 repo prefixes but pallets has 1 instance and mwaskom has 9, while django is 652/1699. Any judge who downloads the file catches that in one command.

Three smaller wounds. (a) The baseline is handed the gold patch and the FAIL_TO_PASS bodies — the two most informative artifacts — so the headroom the advanced solution can claim is compressed before he starts; a null result is a live possibility and Measured Improvement is 15 points that reward demonstrated gains. (b) The mandatory removed experiment ("include experiments you later removed and explain what they taught you") is nowhere in the proposal. (c) precision@40 on the test-fairness criterion has a 0.537 random floor; the claim that it is "hard to game" is overstated, and reporting 0.70 without the floor would read as misleading once a judge computes it.

Finally, "buildable in 28h: comfortably" is wrong. Adequate power needs ~400-500 held-out instances x 2 arms plus dev iterations — order 1,200-1,500 agent invocations — on top of shallow-cloning 12 large repos (django, sympy, scikit-learn, matplotlib, sphinx...) at pinned commits, plus a spec-lens that attempts patch reconstruction per item, plus a reviewer UI, plus 12 hours of video/repro/trajectory packaging. Note that the ready-made HF codebase-content datasets (ScalingIntelligence/swe-bench-verified-codebase-content) cover only the Verified 500 — i.e. exactly the CLEAN items — so he must clone for every severe instance. There is no shortcut on the expensive half.
scores.what_would_make_it_win:
Five changes, in strict priority order. The first two are not optional — without them this is a 75 that loses to a cleaner 85.

1. KILL THE CONTAMINATION OBJECTION BY LEADING WITH IT. Run the memorization probe as changelog Iteration 0 and publish the number: "ranking by recalled SWE-bench-Verified membership scores precision 0.867 on test-fairness, above the 0.804 a paid professional reaches — so I stripped instance_id, repo name, and base_commit SHA from every agent input and re-ran." Report blinded vs unblinded as two arms. Add a direct recall probe (ask the model to classify held-out IDs as Verified/not, report accuracy) as evidence the blinding was necessary. This converts the torpedo into the single most credible artifact in the submission, and it IS the hot take: the correction to the ruler is itself keyed by a public list the models have memorized.

2. FIX THE POWER. Move to >=400 held-out instances, compute the primary metric POOLED with a bootstrap 95% CI, and use the 12+ cases as reporting strata only (say so explicitly, and say why — "per-case Spearman at n=10 has sd 0.31, so I report it pooled"). Stratify proportionally by repo, or by difficulty x criterion; drop the impossible one-repo-per-case scheme (pallets has 1 instance). Keeping the PDF's >=10-cases requirement while explaining the pooling is a credibility gain, not a risk.

3. SHIP THE FIVE-ROW SCOREBOARD. Random floor (0.301 / 0.537 precision@40; ~0 Spearman) / baseline / agent / single paid human by leave-one-out (Spearman 0.376 / 0.455; precision@40 0.474 / 0.804) / oracle (0.99 / 1.00). Ten minutes of pandas. Without it his headline Spearman of ~0.30 reads as failure; with it, it reads as near-human on a task where humans agree weakly. This is also the strongest possible answer to "what does a good result look like for the intended user" — pre-register the target as a fraction of the human ceiling BEFORE running, which the PDF explicitly requires and the proposal currently omits.

4. USE THE DATA'S OWN TIMESTAMPS, DROP THE STOPWATCH. claimed_at -> submitted_at gives median 119 min per annotation across n=3,636 real panel annotations. Report it as a wall-clock upper bound, keep his own 10-item timing as a focused-time lower bound, label which is which. Self-timing alone on a task where he knows the answers is the weakest evidence in the plan and the easiest to attack.

5. UPGRADE THE 13TH CASE AND THE ARTIFACT. Hand-label the 20 fresh scraped issues himself against OpenAI's published rubric (cdn.openai.com/introducing-swe-bench-verified/swe-b-annotation-instructions.pdf, live, HTTP 200) so the one out-of-distribution, provably uncontaminated case produces a NUMBER rather than a vibe — it is now the most important case in the eval, not a footnote. And build the reviewer view: issue text with the quoted anchor highlighted beside the test assertion it fails to justify, plus the disagreement marker. That is 3-4 hours of static HTML from JSON, it is what makes End-to-End Quality read as a tool rather than a spreadsheet, and it is the shot the video needs.

Scope cuts to pay for the above: precompute and cache repo context deterministically ONCE per instance so agent calls become parallel text-in/text-out (this is what makes 400x2 affordable); do not have the spec-lens actually write a patch, have it enumerate the decisions a patch would force; ship cached raw agent outputs plus a scoring script that regenerates the headline table in seconds, with a separate "run 10 live" path, so a judge can verify without paying for 800 calls. And write the removed experiment into the plan now — the honest candidate is the repo-context arm on the underspecification criterion, which I would predict adds little because the issue text plus gold patch already saturates that signal.

scores.candidate_name: Verdict — merging agent code when there is no oracle
scores.strongest_argument_for: The label provenance, and it is the one thing here that cannot be faked. Ground rule 09 and the 15-pt Reproducibility row both reward evidence a judge can verify without trusting the contestant. Nearly every competing "agent reviews code" entry will plant its own bugs and grade its own catches — a self-graded exam. This one does not: the bug is real, the patch was written by someone else's agent, and the resolved/unresolved verdict came out of SWE-bench's own harness run by someone else. A judge can spot-check three instance IDs against a public repo in two minutes and confirm it. Secondary but real: abstention is a structural answer to ground rules 04 and 05 rather than a bolted-on disclaimer — `hold` is a scored outcome that costs the system on its own metric, which is a different and better thing than "a human reviews the output." And the capability discipline (four capabilities with named jobs, no memory, no orchestration) is exactly what §2's "purposeful choices matter more than the number of components" clause rewards.
scores.strongest_argument_against: The primary metric is gameable in precisely the direction the proposal claims it is closed, and the flaw sits inside the sentence defending it. Coverage is defined over decisions (merge + reject); precision is defined over merges only. On 120 triples at ~50/50, a system can output reject on 68, merge on the 4 most obviously-correct one-line patches, and hold on 48: coverage = 72/120 = 60%, clearing the floor; precision = 4/4 = 100%. It merged 4 of ~60 mergeable patches, saved the reviewer nothing, and posted a perfect headline. The stated guard — "abstaining broadly collapses coverage below the floor" — does not bite, because rejects count as coverage. Compounding it: the baseline→final gap will likely be dominated by the disclosed resource difference (the advanced solution reads the repo, the baseline reads two pasted texts), not by the spec-before-patch ordering that is the entire hot take — so the headline number may be both attackable and attributable to something other than the idea. And SWE-bench contamination is unaddressed: the corpus is django/sympy/sklearn/matplotlib, whose post-fix state is in the model's training data, so "derive the spec from the issue alone" may be recall rather than derivation. That is the first question micro1's own judges — an agent-evaluation lab — will ask.
scores.what_would_make_it_win: Seven changes, all instrumentation and framing rather than new building, and all affordable if the Docker experiment is cut. (1) Replace the coverage floor with a pre-committed merge-recall floor: report precision at fixed merge-recall, or pre-commit the full triple (merge-precision, merge-recall, hold-rate). Ten minutes of thought; converts the weakest sentence into the strongest. (2) Run a contamination probe (~2h): given only the issue and the repo at base commit, ask the model to state the fix and measure agreement with the gold patch. Report the number and caveat it. Almost nobody else will measure this, and unaddressed it lets a judge discount everything. (3) Build the harness paired from hour one and use McNemar on paired disagreements, not independent proportions — on ~72 decided cases the unpaired CI half-width is roughly ±10 points, so a 5-point ordering effect is invisible without pairing. (4) Replace the two cheat probes (which will fire near-zero times on leaderboard predictions, since those never touch test files) with a deterministic battery that actually fires: does the patch apply cleanly with git apply, do modified files still ast.parse, does it touch the symbol the issue names, does it touch unrelated files. ~2h, genuinely predictive, and it instantiates his own signature move — enforce in code, not in prompts. The null cheat-probe result then becomes a free honest removed-experiment row. (5) Cut Docker entirely or timebox it to 90 minutes; a pre-announced expected failure is theater, and the ablation ladder produces real removed experiments for free. (6) Build one genuinely well-finished user-facing artifact — a review card showing the derived spec, clause-by-clause scoring, deterministic check results, verdict, confidence, and the one thing to check if held — because 20 points ride on "would the intended user consider this high quality" and the proposal currently describes a study, not a product. (7) Lead the hot take with a measured number, not the aphorism: "showing the patch first flipped N of 120 verdicts, all toward merge." That measurement falls out of the A/B he is already running and moves the row from 3 to 5. Two scheduling constraints: time the manual reviewer baseline in hour one, blind to labels, before touching the corpus, or the "reviewer minutes per patch" claim is contaminated and violates ground rule 09; and fetch repos via GitHub's tarball-at-commit API, not git clone — django and sympy do not clone in seconds. With these, the submission lands around 84 and is competitive; as written it is a very good entry that loses to someone whose headline number cannot be attacked.

scores.strongest_argument_for:
The scoring path contains no LLM. Kill/survive is a boolean per mutant produced by executing code, which is a structural credibility advantage in a field where coding-agent use is mandatory and a large share of the 5,100 entries will grade their own agent with an LLM-as-judge. It satisfies ground rule 09 ("connect every claim about your results to the evidence you submit") mechanically rather than rhetorically, and it is the same move the PDF's own Example 1 endorses: "Tie every score to a file, test result or build output." A judge can re-derive the headline number from committed artifacts without trusting the author's taste.

Two engineering details are load-bearing and would survive cross-examination. The pristine-source gate is genuine verification in the PDF's §2 sense — it catches an error before it reaches the user, because a test that fails on unmutated source is a defect being shipped, and it is the single most common real failure of AI test generation. Running each mutant in a subprocess under a timeout shows the author has actually implemented mutation testing rather than read about it; scoring an infinite-loop mutant as a "kill" is the canonical naive-implementation bug and most entrants who reach for mutation testing this weekend will ship it.

The problem and user are concrete, not archetypal. "The PR shows 94% coverage and green and I cannot tell whether these tests would notice a regression" is a sentence a real tech lead has said. And the choice of a manufactured mutant catalog over bug-fix-commit archaeology is correct scoping judgement for a 28-hour build: it produces cases deterministically instead of gambling five hours on repos that may not reproduce.
scores.strongest_argument_against:
Two structural problems, plus one that undermines the centerpiece.

(1) The headline comparison is contaminated and the author appears to know it. The sanctioned baseline is Type 1 — one prompt, no tools, no execution. Its tests are never run, so a large share of them will fail the pristine-source gate and score a hard 0% under the stated rule. The reported delta therefore mostly measures "one arm could execute code and one could not," not "mutation feedback improves test quality." The genuinely informative control — an agent with pytest and coverage, iterating to green, no mutation feedback — is present in the proposal but explicitly demoted: "not the sanctioned baseline, just an exhibit." That is the most informative number in the study being moved to a footnote. The PDF's fairness clause is written verbatim to catch this: "Explain any meaningful difference in the resources available to each one." A judge who reads it will discount the headline heavily, and Measured Improvement is 15 points.

(2) The 20-point End to End row asks whether the intended user would consider the output high quality. The output is generated pytest files. The project has no metric and no mechanism for their readability, brittleness, or reviewability — and the primary metric actively pressures the agent toward implementation-coupled assertions, a failure the proposal predicts about itself in the hard case and then only promises to report verbatim. Honest, and good for the 5-point Hot Take row, but it means the shipped artifact is likely to contain exactly the tests the intended user would reject in review. Worse, no user-facing surface is described at all: no CLI, no diff, no report a lead could act on. As scoped this is an experiment and a results table, which is not "a final result the user can use."

(3) The centerpiece — the held-out split — leaks by construction. Visible and held-out mutants come from the same operator set applied to the same lines, so they are strongly co-located. A test that kills `<` → `<=` at line 42 will very often also kill the held-out `1` → `2` at line 42. The proposal specifies "seeded, committed, ~70/30" and says nothing about stratifying by line or function. So the visible-versus-held-out gap — the number the entire hot take rests on — is likely to come out small for reasons of split design rather than agent quality, and the insight deflates into "held-out splits work, effect was minor."

Secondary but real: the pre-registered ">=70% held-out kill rate" is uncalibrated. Each module has an unknown equivalent-mutant ceiling; if it is 15%, the target is trivial, if 3%, near-impossible. The author cannot know which until after the runs, which hollows out the "define good before you run" discipline that makes the pre-registration credible in the first place. And on held-out mutants the agent cannot file equivalence claims at all, so that floor silently depresses the primary metric by an unreported amount.

On crowding: the proposal calls it medium. A judge's first-pass filter operates at the coarse resolution — "AI writes tests" — which is one of the two or three most obvious lanes when 5,100 engineers are told to pick a developer problem. The mutation-scored, held-out-split refinement is genuinely rare, but it is the fifth sentence, not the first four words.

On time: the 3-hour corpus estimate is the optimistic one. Finding 10-12 PyPI packages that ship runnable offline tests, install without heavy deps, and fit an agent context is realistically 5-7 hours — most sdists ship no tests at all. Every authored starter suite is a case where the author controlled both the initial weakness and the scorer, and a judge may fairly discount those. Meanwhile mutation testing is slow: 3-4 changelog iterations each re-evaluated with the same method means six-plus full sweeps across the corpus. The failure mode is not "no submission," it is a degraded one — 7 cases instead of 11, 2 iterations instead of 4, cross-check dropped — which costs points on explicit checkboxes.
scores.what_would_make_it_win:
Ranked by points-per-hour.

1. Promote the Type-2 control to co-primary (2h of run time, no new code). Report three arms: one-shot prompt with no execution (sanctioned Type 1), an agent with pytest plus coverage iterating to green with no mutation feedback, and Sharpen. Make the headline "c vs b," not "c vs a." This converts "my agent beats a strawman" into "mutation feedback is worth N points of real defect detection," which is the only claim worth making, and it pre-empts the fairness clause instead of tripping it.

2. Split the mutant catalog by code region, not at random (1h). Hold out whole functions or line-blocks so visible and held-out mutants are not co-located. Then say in the changelog that random splitting was tried first and leaked — that is a real removed experiment, which the PDF explicitly requires, and it upgrades the hot take from "train/test splits exist" to "here is how a feedback-signal holdout leaks if you split it wrong."

3. Ship a user surface (2h). `sharpen path/to/module.py` emitting a reviewable diff plus a one-page report — mutants killed, equivalence claims with reasons, suite runtime added. Right now the 20-point row has nothing to grade but a results table. This is the cheapest large gain on the board.

4. Measure the artifact, not only the score (2h). Count generated tests that touch private attributes or assert on call counts, and hand-review five files against a fixed four-item rubric. If mutation pressure degrades test quality, that finding is a better headline than the held-out gap and it lands the hot take on something specific and surprising rather than on rediscovered ML hygiene.

5. Fix the pre-registration before the sweeps (30 min). Replace ">=70% absolute" with a target relative to the Type-2 arm, and hand-adjudicate equivalent mutants on two modules to establish a ceiling. Timestamp it in the repo.

6. Cut scope to buy the above. Drop the third-party mutation-tool cross-check entirely — it costs roughly three hours and yields a caveat ("my engine says 74%, mutmut says 61%") rather than credibility, because the operator sets differ. Freeze the AST engine at six operators by hour three, or just use a pinned mutmut and spend the hours on the agent.

7. Report the pristine gate as a separate number, not a multiplier. Publish held-out kill rate on passing cases alongside cases-passing-the-gate. Folding a hard 0% into a 10-case average creates a cliff that will not reproduce on a judge's machine, and Reproducibility is 15 points.

8. Two smaller ones. Add memory as the iteration-3 capability — accumulate survivor-pattern-to-assertion-pattern knowledge across modules with a wipe-versus-accumulate ablation; that produces the cross-item effect the PDF's Example 3 rewards, and it is more purposeful than a static markdown playbook. And give the repro guide a five-minute two-module fast path, because a judge who sees a forty-minute full sweep will not run it at all.

Do 1, 2, 3 and 5 and this becomes a genuine top-tier entry. Do only what is currently proposed and it is a competent, honest, well-written submission that a judge files next to the other test-generation entries.

scores.candidate_name: Precedent — the grader that does not drift
scores.strongest_argument_for: Memory-as-case-law is a real mechanism on an axis a stateless baseline structurally cannot attempt, and it maps one-to-one onto the PDF's third appendix example ("each sentence can be correct while the series as a whole no longer feels coherent") — a judge who read the appendix recognises the move immediately. The supporting engineering is Chinmoy's signature and the right call: the consistency checker is deterministic code, not a prompt (comparison graph, cycle detection, precedent-contradiction routing), so only contradictions pay for the expensive second pass. The architecture decomposes naturally into exactly the 4-row changelog the PDF leaked, and the hard case (a near-duplicate differing by one planted off-by-one) both justifies the headline feature and indicts the naive version of it — the kind of self-indicting evidence the "include experiments you removed" clause is fishing for. Public dataset with a published human ceiling, disclosed 3x cost, same cases for both arms: the fairness rules are cleanly satisfied. And the judges are literally the intended user — micro1 sells evaluations.
scores.strongest_argument_against: The primary metric has no headroom, and the published literature on this exact corpus says so. lmsys/mt_bench_human_judgments exists because of Zheng et al. 2023, whose headline result is that a single GPT-4 prompt already reaches ~85% agreement on non-tied pairs — matching the ~81% human-human figure the candidate cites as "the ceiling." He is proposing to spend 3x the tokens to reach a ceiling the Type-1 baseline already sits on. At 720 pairs the SE on agreement is ~1.4pp, so any delta under ~3pp is noise, and he is rigorous enough to report CIs, meaning he publishes his own null on the headline. What is left moving is a gate he invented, with no stated threshold and no external anchor (MT-Bench publishes no intra-annotator repeat-consistency rate) — precisely the self-serving-metric trap the PDF warns about. Compounding it: (a) the stated bottleneck is misdiagnosed — "item 200 vs item 3" and "how deep into the batch it sits" describe a human or a context-carrying judge, but the sanctioned Type-1 baseline is one stateless call per item, so at temp 0 there is no positional drift to fix, only a few points of API nondeterminism; (b) order-swap verification is not an improvement over MT-Bench, it IS MT-Bench — the paper measures position bias and FastChat implements the swap, so a third of the advanced solution reimplements the benchmark's own default in front of judges who evaluate agents for a living; (c) the swap mechanically LOWERS agreement, since every order-inconsistent item becomes a forced tie that misses wherever the human had a clear preference. Expected table: agreement ~0 change, self-contradiction −7pp on a self-defined gate, cost 3x. That is a null on the primary metric against a rubric row worded "demonstrates gains over a fair baseline."
scores.what_would_make_it_win: Five changes, the first of which costs zero build hours and is the highest-leverage edit available. (1) FLIP THE METRIC HIERARCHY. Make self-contradiction rate the primary metric and human agreement the guard ("consistency must not be bought by degrading agreement below baseline"). Same two numbers, opposite emphasis — now the baseline has a real number to beat instead of a ceiling it already occupies, and the gate stops looking rigged. State the threshold and its derivation in the README before any run. (2) RUN THE DEGENERATE BASELINES. "Always pick the longer response" has zero order-flips, zero cycles, zero repeat-disagreements and ~65% agreement at 1/3 the cost — it passes the gate trivially. Also run "always follow nearest precedent, never distinguish." Both are ~20 lines, both are his documented habit of shipping deliberately weak baselines, and without them a judge invents the length attack in ten seconds and the gate reads as naive. (3) RUN THE ONE EXPERIMENT NOBODY ELSE WILL HAVE: does the precedent store harden a bias into doctrine? If early rulings encode verbosity bias, "follow or distinguish" bootstraps it into case law and agreement on short-correct-answer cases should decay as the store fills. Measurable, cheap, unclaimed — and it is the honest version of the hot take, which should become "memory makes a judge coherent and confidently wrong at the same time" rather than the already-known "your judge is unreliable, not biased." (4) FIX TWO CONTAMINATIONS AND ONE GATE RISK: move mirror images OUT of the batch that seeds the precedent store (otherwise the nearest retrieved case for item N is item N's own mirror, and consistency inflates for a reason unrelated to the mechanism); ship a cached-transcript replay mode plus a 20-item smoke run so judges reproduce at zero cost and get the README's exact numbers — a project about reproducible judgement that cannot reproduce its own is fatal irony; and route the contradictions queue to an explicit HUMAN reviewer, because a grade that decides a payment or rejection triggers ground rule 05 and the trajectory deliverable asks for human checkpoints anyway. Verify the dataset licence string against the actual card in hour 1 — if NC, micro1's ownership-plus-training clause is commercial use, and switch to MIT-licensed hh-rlhf before anything is built on it. (5) CUT THE CORPUS from 720 pairs to ~240 (6 batches of 40) — the PDF requires ten cases, not seven hundred — and spend the reclaimed hours on the consistency report artifact and on re-centering the user story on the PERSON WHO WAS GRADED rather than the ops lead, which converts a self-referential AI-tool-for-AI-people into something with a human on the receiving end. Done all five, this is an 82-85 and a real contender for Best Engineering Workflow; done none, it is a well-written 70 with a null headline.

scores.strongest_argument_for: The headline number is a physical measurement, not an LLM's opinion about an LLM. Nearly every one of the ~500-1,000 completed submissions will report a metric produced by a model judging model output; §6's Measured Improvement (15) and Reproducibility (15) rows, plus tie-breaks #2 and #3, reward the one entry where a judge types one command and watches a stopwatch produce the same verdicts. The eval needs no network, no API key, no service, no historical test suite to resurrect — that clears the §9 qualification gate ("a project that cannot be run or verified may be disqualified before rubric scoring") more cleanly than almost any LLM-judge design.
