Rule 04 is satisfied by the architecture itself, not by a paragraph: every edit lands in an isolated worktree and is reverted by default, so the consequential action never happens without evidence. And the hot take is the best element in the proposal — "whenever an agent's claim is cheap to verify with a tool and expensive to verify by reading, the tool must be inside the loop, not the review afterwards, because the explanation will be equally fluent either way" is exactly what the 5-point row asks for: an observed failure mode converted into a transferable building rule. It is also memorable, which matters when a judge is scoring their two-hundredth entry.
scores.strongest_argument_against:
The improvement is manufactured by the experimental design rather than discovered, and it is manufactured twice over.

First, the baseline is denied a stopwatch and then scored with a stopwatch. The proposal states this as a virtue — "the only withheld resource is measurement, which makes the attribution unambiguous" — but §3's fairness clause governs the row this project exists to win, and a judge reading "I removed measurement from the baseline, then measured" sees a tautology, not an experiment. The objection is concrete: a Type-2 general-purpose agent in 2026 has bash. `python -m timeit`, or three lines of `time.perf_counter`, is inside any real baseline's reach. The delta is not "agents can't measure" but "I told this one not to."

Second, the magnitude of "trusted speedup" is a number the author chooses when he writes the corpus, not one he discovers. Six of twelve cases are self-authored around named archetypes — N+1 lookup, quadratic string building, regex recompiled in a hot path, dict rebuilt per iteration, JSON re-parsed per record, sort inside a scan. Every one of those is a textbook win at every realistic input size, which means a frontier model gets all six right *without measuring*. The baseline will score close to the solution on half the corpus by construction. The proposal defends against the wrong adversary: it argues at length that the *agent* cannot game the metric, and never addresses that the *author* sets its value by choosing what fruit to plant.

Third, the metric's own arithmetic works against the story. Scoring a correctness failure as 1.00x is lenient, not punitive — it treats "shipped broken code" identically to "did nothing." A baseline that breaks 4 cases and gets 3x on the other 8 still reports (3^8)^(1/12) = 2.08x. The likely result table is roughly 2.4x vs 2.0x — a ~20% delta — while the actual story (0 regressions and 0 correctness failures vs 4-5) sits in a side column labeled "guards." The solution's floor is 1.00x by construction, so the primary metric never measures capability; it measures whether the revert logic works, which any implementation achieves. Meanwhile the number that would sell this — human time per case, ~20 min of hand-benchmarking 12 unverified diffs down to ~2 min of reading evidence — is relegated to a supporting row because §5 asks for it. The primary metric is the weakest of the four numbers this project will produce.

Two further specifics. The hard case is fragile: NumPy per-call overhead is ~1-5 microseconds and a 40-element Python loop is ~2-4 microseconds, so the case sits directly on the crossover, and its direction is a function of NumPy version, BLAS, and memory subsystem. On the judge's machine the centerpiece narrative may invert and the "textbook optimization is a regression" case becomes a win, on camera. And the corpus format smuggles in the hard half of the real problem: every case ships with a workload generator, a pinned baseline, and a hand-authored invariant test — the three artifacts a real user with a 40-minute batch job does not have. The invariant test is written by the person who planted the trap it catches, which is circular in a way a judge will name.
scores.what_would_make_it_win:
Seven changes, in descending leverage. The first two are the difference between ~69 and a submission in the conversation.

1. UNCRIPPLE THE BASELINE, AND MAKE ITS FAILURE AN EMPIRICAL FINDING. Give the Type-2 baseline full bash and full freedom, and let it decide whether to measure. The result stops being "I withheld a tool" and becomes a discovery: "given a shell and no instruction to use it, the agent measured in 2 of 12 cases, misread the timing in 1, and shipped 5 confident regressions." That is a finding about agent behavior — micro1's actual business — instead of an artifact of the harness. It removes the fairness objection entirely and converts the weakest row into the strongest. Run both baselines if time allows (Type 1 prompt-only, Type 2 with bash); the two-rung ladder is cheap and shows the improvement is not an accident of one configuration.

2. DEMOTE TRUSTED SPEEDUP. Make the primary metric something the author's corpus choices cannot inflate: trustworthy-edit rate — of the edits each system retains, what fraction are genuinely faster AND correct when independently re-benchmarked. Baseline 7/12 retained, 2 genuinely faster; solution 7/7. That number is not set by how much fruit you plant, it survives a judge swapping in their own cases, and it produces a poster figure instead of a 20% ratio. Keep trusted speedup as the secondary, and pre-register both.

3. DEFEND TIE-BREAK #2 WITH A DETERMINISTIC LAYER. Wall-clock will not reproduce on the judge's hardware and the README must say so first, before the judge discovers it. Report decision agreement — which of the 12 edits were kept versus reverted — as the invariant that reproduces, ship a Dockerfile with a pinned Python and NumPy, print a machine-profile line at the top of every run, and have the harness self-check the hard case's crossover and warn loudly if it has moved on this machine. Also: build on Windows, verify in WSL or Docker before submitting. Budget an hour for it; worktrees and subprocess paths are where it breaks.

4. REPLACE HAND-AUTHORED INVARIANT TESTS WITH DIFFERENTIAL TESTING. Run original versus optimized on randomized inputs and compare outputs exactly. It is a generic oracle that would exist on a real user's code, it kills the "you wrote the gate for the trap you planted" objection, and it is less work than authoring 12 property tests.

5. RUN IT ONCE ON A REAL REPO, ON VIDEO. One unplanted case where the tool finds a real win in code the author did not write does more against the synthetic-corpus objection than any paragraph. Put it in the 5-minute video as the realistic execution §8.03 demands.

6. CONFRONT PRIOR ART IN ONE HONEST PARAGRAPH. asv, pytest-benchmark, hyperfine, codspeed, the autotuner lineage (OpenTuner, Halide autoschedulers), and the published measured-speedup benchmarks for LLM code edits. "Measure, keep if faster, revert if not" is the definition of an autotuner; the defensible claim is that the loop lives inside the agent rather than in an offline eval of its outputs. Silence here reads as unawareness and costs points on Problem and End-to-End Quality both.

7. ABLATE THE MEMORY LEDGER AND PUBLISH THE NULL RESULT. Within a single session the agent already has its own transcript, so the rejected-hypothesis file is probably redundant with context and will likely show no effect. §4 makes a removed experiment mandatory and warns that an all-wins changelog reads as fabricated. This is the cheapest honest negative result available and it is already sitting in the design — plan it rather than discovering it at hour 60.

Two schedule corrections. Corpus assembly is budgeted at 4-5 hours and will take 10-12: finding pure-Python OSS code that is genuinely slow, self-contained, permissively licensed, and has or needs tests is an hour of browsing per case. Vendor those six modules with their LICENSE files rather than fetching pinned versions at setup — network at setup is friction on Rule 10 for no gain. And the eval itself is serial wall-clock the author cannot work through: keep per-trial workloads at 0.2-0.5s so a full 12-case two-arm run finishes in ten minutes, because §4 requires the same evaluation method at every changelog row and there will be four or five of them.

scores.strongest_argument_for: This is one of very few hackathon problems where "did the agent get it right" can have MECHANICAL ground truth rather than an LLM judge, and the rubric pays 30 pts for exactly that ("uses agents purposefully and is technically sound", "verification: catch errors before they reach the user") plus 15 more for a defensible measured delta. The user is real and the bottleneck is the defining engineering complaint of 2026: teams merging AI-written code cannot tell what a green CI badge is worth. It is also culturally on-message with the judges — micro1's stated business is "evaluating AI agents" and "reliable, accurate, useful", and this is a tool that measures whether AI-written code is trustworthy. Finally, the proposer's documented habits (defect-pins that fail-on-old/pass-on-fix, committed evidence scripts, deliberately-reported weak baselines, publishing unwanted answers) are an unusually good fit for the Measured Improvement and Reproducibility rows, which are tie-breaks #3 and #2.
scores.strongest_argument_against: Two independent kill shots. (1) CROWDING: "multi-agent code reviewer" is the single most duplicated artifact in the agentic ecosystem — it is the modal submission for a field of 5,100 engineers required to use coding agents, and it competes against free one-click incumbents (CodeRabbit, Greptile, Cursor BugBot, Qodo) that the proposal never benchmarks against, leaving "why would a real person use this instead" unanswered. Tie-break #1 is the Agent Solution row, i.e. you must be top-3 in the most fatigued category the judges will read. (2) THE METRIC IS BOTH GAMEABLE AND STATISTICALLY EMPTY AS SPECIFIED. No clean-diff negative-control population is named, so ~100% of cases contain a planted bug in a small diff — an agent that emits "there is a bug" unconditionally scores near-100% catch rate. The only thing preventing that is the FP guard, and the proposal gives it no threshold, no denominator, no per-case flag/no-flag decision rule, and no file:line localization requirement. At n=10 the catch rate carries roughly a +/-15pp confidence interval, so any delta under ~3 cases is inside LLM run-to-run noise, and no variance reporting is planned. Compounding this: surviving mutants are by construction lodged in code the suite does not discriminate (dead code, logging, defensive branches), and "the suite must still pass" does not screen equivalent mutants — semantic no-ops enter the corpus labeled as defects, so the ground truth itself is wrong on an unknown fraction of cases. Separately, "every finding must state a concrete failure scenario" is LLM prose adjudicated by LLM prose; models are excellent at writing convincing stories about bugs that do not exist, so the skeptic stage as designed amplifies confabulation instead of filtering it. And the hot take — "a green test suite is not evidence of correctness" — is Dijkstra 1969, the most-quoted line in software engineering, and it is a lesson about test suites when the 5-pt row explicitly asks for "a practical lesson for building more reliable agents."
scores.what_would_make_it_win: Six changes, roughly in order of points-per-hour. (1) REPLACE PROSE VERIFICATION WITH EXECUTION. Every surviving finding must ship a runnable probe that FAILS on current code and PASSES on the proposed fix; run both, auto-discard anything that does not flip. This is the proposer's own documented "defect-pin" discipline and his signature "enforce in code, not in the prompt." It converts the system from LLM-opinions-filtered-by-LLM-opinions into claims-filtered-by-execution, drives false positives toward zero by construction, and is the single change that moves the 30-pt row from ~19 to ~26. Reframe the whole project around this, not around the personas. (2) ADD CLEAN CONTROLS AND PRE-REGISTER THE DECISION RULE. At least as many defect-free diffs as defect-bearing ones, shuffled so they are indistinguishable; per case the system must emit block/pass; a finding counts only if it names the right file and line; pre-register the ceiling in writing before running ("<=1 false blocker per 10 clean diffs, else the run fails"). Without this the primary metric is not defensible and Measured Improvement stays around 8. (3) DO NOT BUILD THE HISTORICAL-COMMIT CORPUS. Take BugsInPy or SWE-bench-verified PASS_TO_PASS instances where someone else already solved the environment problem, and select for "pre-existing suite green at the buggy commit" — that IS the premise, already computed. This buys back 8+ hours, and spend them on (1) and (2). Then push the corpus to 25-30 cases (seeded ones are nearly free); the PDF says ten is a floor, and n=10 is statistically useless for a rate. Screen equivalent mutants explicitly and report how many you discarded — that discard count is itself a credibility asset. (4) RUN THE BUDGET-MATCHED CONTROL. Same single prompt sampled 8x with findings unioned, versus the multi-lens architecture at equal token spend. The PDF demands disclosure of resource differences. If the architecture does not beat best-of-N union, that is the honest and most interesting result in the submission and belongs in the changelog as the removed experiment — it is exactly the "publishes unwanted answers" instinct the dossier identifies as his edge. (5) DERIVE THE LENSES FROM OBSERVED BASELINE FAILURES, NEVER UPFRONT. Run the baseline first, categorize its misses, then split lenses along the observed miss categories. "money/security/reliability/data-integrity" chosen in advance reads as generated and violates the changelog's demand that each iteration be motivated by evidence. (6) REPLACE THE HOT TAKE. Drop the Dijkstra restatement. The sharp, on-target finding already sitting in his own data is that the REPAIR loop is itself a defect source — roughly 29% of blockers (5 of 17) were regressions introduced by the previous round's own fix. That is an observed failure mode turned into a lesson about building more reliable agents, which is verbatim what the row asks for, and it justifies a concrete design rule: never seal a fix without re-running the full gate against the fix itself. Two further guards: ship recorded per-case agent outputs plus frozen fixtures so a judge reproduces the headline number in under 15 minutes without network or LLM spend, and report the eval run 3x with the spread — nobody else will, and it directly serves tie-breaks #2 and #3. Demote the Nistula 17-defect anecdote to a single labeled-unverifiable paragraph under "why I chose this problem" and keep it out of every results surface. Even with all six, crowding is not solved: the title still reads as the 80th code-review agent, so the README's first sentence must lead with the execution-grounded probe mechanism and the falsifiable claim, not with "multi-agent review."
